extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of public relations and organizational communication
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the Excellence theory's criteria for what makes public relations effective within organizations, including models, organizational conditions, and measurable dimensions for PR practice and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of public relations lies in organization-public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of public relations lies in organization-public relations: good relationships with strategic publics help an organization develop and achieve goals desired by both the organization and its publics, reduce costs of negative publicity, and increase revenue by providing products and services needed by stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maximize PR value, identify strategic publics and build long-term relationships; measure PR impact by its contribution to organizational goals, cost reductions from avoided negative publicity, and revenue or stakeholder satisfaction gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify strategic publics and build long-term relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must identify strategic publics and build long-term relationships with them through symmetrical communication programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment publics (see situational theory) and design communication programs aimed at relationship-building rather than one-way persuasion; prioritize long-term relationship metrics over short-term campaign outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization's reputation as byproduct of organizational behaviors and relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization's reputation is largely a byproduct of organizational behaviors and organization–public relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PR by how organizational behaviors and relationship management generate reputation; integrate reputation outcomes into strategic management and governance assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowerment of the public relations function
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective organizations must empower public relations as a critical management function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether PR has managerial influence, resources, access to senior leadership, and participation in strategic decision-making rather than being limited to administrative tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicator roles: managerial as well as administrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations executives should be allowed to play managerial roles as well as administrative roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate role breadth—whether PR practitioners are involved in strategy, planning, and management (managerial) rather than only executing communications (administrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of the communication function: integrated and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should be an integrated communication function and separate from, instead of being sublimated to, marketing or other management functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organizational structure: an integrated PR function (coordinating internal/external communication) that retains strategic independence from marketing or other departments indicates higher excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetrical communication model
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective organizations should base their internal and external communication and relationship building on the two-way symmetrical model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor dialogic, balanced communication that attempts mutual understanding and accommodation; measure reciprocity, feedback mechanisms, and mutual adjustment rather than only message distribution or persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal-attainment approach to effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations are effective when they meet their goals (goal-attainment approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use management-by-objectives thinking: ensure PR activities align with organizational aims and that all actors understand objectives and their roles in achieving them; evaluate PR by its contribution to goal attainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems approach: openness and environmental linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations are open systems linked to resources in their external environment; organizational effectiveness recognizes mutual need between an organization and its environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PR by how well it mediates import/export of resources, adapts to environmental change, and maintains linkages with external stakeholders and systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic constituencies approach: identify supportive or threatening elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategic constituencies approach identifies elements of the environment whose opposition or support can threaten or help attain organizational goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map constituencies whose support/opposition matters; apply situational theory to classify publics (nonpublic, latent, aware, active) and prioritize PR efforts accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational theory of publics / public segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: People can be identified and classified according to problem awareness and information-seeking behavior (nonpublic, latent public, aware public, active public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use situational variables (problem recognition, constraint recognition, involvement) to segment audiences and tailor communication strategies to each segment's readiness and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing values model of organizational effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational effectiveness can be evaluated along competing values: Stability vs. Flexibility; Internal vs. External; Means vs. Ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess PR's fit with organizational values—e.g., whether PR supports control and order versus adaptability, prioritizes internal well-being versus external development, or emphasizes processes versus outcomes—and choose evaluation criteria accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global public relations theory: adapt practice to national context
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence theory extends into a global theory that offers generic principles but suggests practice should differ based on culture, political/economic system, media system, level of economic development, and nature of activism in a country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying excellence criteria cross-culturally, adjust expectations and practices to national context; validate measures (e.g., via replication studies) before assuming universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal influence model (non-Western practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may build personal influence with key individuals (government regulators, media, tax officials) by doing favors so they can solicit favors in return; this model plays a dominant role in many developing countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize alternative (non-Western) models of PR where interpersonal patronage and personal influence are primary mechanisms; evaluation should account for culturally-specific practices rather than imposing Western managerial norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations measurable scales (Laskin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laskin proposed measurable scales: direction of communication scale, intended beneficiary scale, strategic nature scale, role scale, and timeframe scale to capture communication concepts and balance of intended effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuous, measurable scales to operationalize PR constructs; adapt the set of scales (add/drop) to capture peculiarities of a specific campaign, organization, or industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency/continuum critique of pure symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The two-way symmetrical model may be unrealistic; symmetrical communication works along a continuum from pure conflict to pure cooperation, and true excellence may result from picking the appropriate point along that continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply contingency thinking: select communication stances appropriate to situation, time, and power relations rather than insisting on pure symmetry; evaluate excellence by fit to context rather than by an absolute ideal of symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: consider cultural difference and power inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence theory may underpin and perpetuate inequalities of power by imposing a monocultural and normative management model, potentially devaluing national traditions, minorities, and cultural differences and subordinating societal wellbeing to corporate profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging PR practice, assess whether recommended models respect cultural diversity and power dynamics; include equity and societal wellbeing as evaluative dimensions, not just organizational effectiveness or profitability.
